hints: Think about how an unreactive alkane like ethane can have a C-H bond replaced by C-Br, and what type of energy is needed to split $\text{Br}_2$ into radicals.
walkthrough:
Spot the change from ethane to A**
Look closely at the structures. Ethane $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3$ becomes $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$. Two H atoms have been replaced by two Br atoms. Alkanes only do substitution with halogens by a radical route.

Recall the radical conditions**
$\text{Br-Br}$ needs to be broken homolytically to give $\text{Br}^\bullet$ radicals to start the chain. That needs UV light, or strong heat. So the reagent is $\text{Br}_2$ plus UV light.
Final answer: Bromine, $\text{Br}_2$, with UV light (or sunlight or high temperature/heat).

hints: A is 1,2-dibromoethane with Br on different carbons, so draw the only other way to place two Br atoms on a two carbon chain with the same formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Br}_2$.
walkthrough:
Count the ways to get $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Br}_2$**
A has one Br on each carbon. The only other arrangement with the same molecular formula is to put both Br atoms on the same carbon. That gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBr}_2$, which is a positional isomer of A.
Final answer: 1,1-dibromoethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBr}_2$.

hints: Work backwards from butanedioic acid $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and remember that each $\text{CN}$ group adds one carbon then hydrolyses to $\text{COOH}$.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the diacid**
The final product has 4 carbons, but A only has 2 carbons. Step 2 must add one carbon at each end. The classic way to do that is to replace each Br with $\text{CN}$, because $\text{CN}$ can then be hydrolysed in step 3 to $\text{COOH}$. So B must be $\text{NC-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CN}$.
Final answer: $\text{NCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ (butanedinitrile).

hints: Identify the reaction type when Br in a bromoalkane is replaced by $\text{CN}$ to extend the chain.
Recall why this substitution must be heated under reflux in ethanol rather than in aqueous solution, to favour substitution over elimination or hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
Name the nucleophile**
You are swapping $\text{C-Br}$ for $\text{C-CN}$. That is nucleophilic substitution by cyanide ion. So use potassium or sodium cyanide, $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$, which provides $\text{CN}^-$.

Choose conditions to favour substitution**
Haloalkanes with $\text{CN}^-$ need heating under reflux. The solvent must be ethanol, not water. In water $\text{OH}^-$ would compete and give an alcohol. Ethanolic $\text{KCN}$ with heat gives the dinitrile cleanly.

Final answer: Reagent: $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ or $\text{CN}^-$.
Conditions: heat / boil / reflux in ethanol (ethanolic solution).

hints: Think of the two familiar purple and orange oxidants used warm and acidified to oxidise reducing agents like $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and ethanedioate.
walkthrough:
Recall the common warm aqueous oxidants**
In A Level chemistry the two standard oxidants are acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$. Ethanedioic acid, $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$, is a reducing agent that decolourises warm acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$. Either named oxidant is accepted here.
Final answer: Acidified potassium manganate(VII), $\text{KMnO}_4$, or acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$.

hints: Consider what happens when $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$ is fully oxidised, each carbon is already highly oxidised so it breaks down to the simplest oxide of carbon plus water.
walkthrough:
Follow the carbons to full oxidation**
Ethanedioic acid has only two carbons, both as $\text{COOH}$. Strong oxidation cleaves the C-C bond and each carbon becomes $\text{CO}_2$. The H atoms form $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The equation is $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H} + [O] \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Final answer: Carbon dioxide, $\text{CO}_2$, and water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Order the three by how easily they release $\text{H}^+$, remembering carboxylic acids are stronger than phenols which are stronger than alcohols.
Think about what stabilises the negative ion left behind, comparing the extra electronegative O in $\text{RCOOH}$ with the benzene ring in phenol.
Consider how an alkyl group pushes electrons toward O in hexan-1-ol and how that affects the O-H bond strength and the alkoxide ion stability.
walkthrough:
Link acidity to anion stability**
Acidity is $\text{HA} \rightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$. The more stable the anion $\text{A}^-$, the further right the equilibrium lies and the stronger the acid. So compare $\text{RCOO}^-$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ and $\text{RO}^-$.

Explain the carboxylic acid strength**
In hexanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, the carbonyl O is very electronegative. It pulls electron density away from the O-H bond, making it weaker and easier to break. After loss of $\text{H}^+$, the negative charge is delocalised over two O atoms in $\text{RCO}_2^-$. That excellent stabilisation makes it the strongest.

Explain the middle position of phenol**
In phenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, the lone pair on O overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This delocalisation weakens the O-H bond slightly. More importantly, the phenoxide ion $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ has its negative charge delocalised into the ring. This stabilises it, but less than the carboxylate, so phenol is weaker than the acid but stronger than the alcohol.

Explain why the alcohol is weakest**
In hexan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{OH}$, the alkyl group is electron donating. It pushes electron density onto O, strengthening the O-H bond and intensifying the negative charge on $\text{RO}^-$. With no delocalisation to spread the charge, the alkoxide is unstable, so the alcohol hardly releases $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: Most acidic: hexanoic acid > phenol > hexan-1-ol : least acidic.
Hexanoic acid: the C=O oxygen withdraws electron density, weakens O-H and stabilises the carboxylate anion, $\text{RCO}_2^-$.
Phenol: the benzene ring delocalises the lone pair on O / negative charge on phenoxide ion, stabilising the anion and weakening O-H, but less effectively than the carboxylate.
Hexan-1-ol: alkyl group donates electrons, strengthens O-H and destabilises the alkoxide anion.

hints: Recall which proton appears very far downfield near $\delta$ 11 to 13 due to strong deshielding by two electronegative O atoms.
Compare the two remaining alkyl signals at $\delta$ 3.3 and $\delta$ 1.1, deciding which is the CH next to two $\text{C=O}$ groups and which is the $\text{CH}_3$ group.
walkthrough:
Assign the very low field singlet**
$\delta$ 12.7 is characteristic of a carboxylic acid $\text{O-H}$. The H is attached to O bonded to $\text{C=O}$, so it is highly deshielded. In $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ the two $\text{COOH}$ groups are equivalent enough to give one signal.

Assign the alkyl signals by deshielding**
The CH proton sits directly between two electron withdrawing $\text{C=O}$ groups, so it is more deshielded and appears at $\delta$ 3.3. The $\text{CH}_3$ protons are further away and more shielded, so they appear at $\delta$ 1.1.

Final answer: $\delta$ 12.7: $\text{COOH}$ protons (the two acid OH protons).
$\delta$ 3.3: CH proton (the $\text{CH}$ bonded to $\text{CH}_3$ and two $\text{C=O}$).
$\delta$ 1.1: $\text{CH}_3$ protons.

hints: Count the lines in the $\delta$ 3.3 signal and use the n+1 rule to link it to the number of equivalent H atoms on the adjacent carbon.
walkthrough:
Apply the n+1 rule**
The signal at $\delta$ 3.3 has four lines, a quartet. The CH proton has as its neighbour the $\text{CH}_3$ group with 3 equivalent protons. Using n+1, 3+1 = 4 lines. Coupling to the $\text{COOH}$ protons does not occur due to exchange.
Final answer: Quartet (quadruplet) due to 3 H / protons on the neighbouring / adjacent $\text{CH}_3$ carbon (n+1 = 4).

hints: Look for symmetry in $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ versus $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and count distinct carbon environments in each.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbons using symmetry**
Butanedioic acid $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ is symmetric. The two $\text{C=O}$ carbons are identical and the two $\text{CH}_2$ carbons are identical, so 2 environments give 2 peaks. Methylpropanedioic acid $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ has two $\text{C=O}$ carbons identical, plus one CH carbon plus one $\text{CH}_3$ carbon, so 3 environments give 3 peaks.
Final answer: Butanedioic acid: 2 peaks. Methylpropanedioic acid: 3 peaks.
